original: Au soir, quant il orent mengié, dist Neronneus a Lanselot: «Sire, vous vous departirés demain de chaiens et je sai bien que vous tournerés vers le grant cemin au plus tost que vous porrés. Et pour ce que je sai bien tout vraiement que vous ne savés que vous trouverés ça avant, vous en voel je acointier une partie.
gold_trans: That evening, after eating, Neroneus said to Lancelot: “Sire, you will leave this place tomorrow and I know well that you will rejoin the main road as soon as you can. And since you do not know what you will find there, I will acquaint you with a part of it.”
baseline_trans: At evening, when they had eaten, Neronneus said to Lancelot: "Sir, you will depart from here tomorrow and I know well that you will turn towards the great road as soon as you can. And because I know well truly that you do not know what you will find there, I will acquaint you with a part of it.

original: Sachiés que vous trouverés demain entour eure de prime, cha devant en une montaingne, un castel fort et rice de grant maniere. En celui castel a orendroit tout nouvelement mise avant une coustume assés anieuse et vilainne, dont maint anui venront encore et maint grant mal en seront fait, s’ele est longement maintenue.
gold_trans: Be aware that after prime, you will see tomorrow a mountain where a magnificent fortified castle stands. This castle is subject to a rather dangerous and offensive custom from which many more unpleasant consequences will arise. And many serious problems will arise from this if it is maintained for a long time.
baseline_trans: Be aware that you will find tomorrow surrounded by dawn, in a mountain, a strong and beautiful castle. In that castle, a very unpleasant and vile custom has recently been introduced, from which many evils will come and many great misfortunes will be done, if it is maintained for a long time.
note: “beautiful” added; “magnificent/fortified” lost + entour eure de prime

original: Car bien sachiés que tout li cevalier errant ki de la maison le roi Artu sont et ki vienent cele part i sont aresté et retenu et mis em prison, ce m’est avis; et autresi retienent il les damoiseles conmunaument qu’il truevent alant en conduit de cevalier, qui que il soit.
gold_trans: For you should know that all knights-errant belonging to King Arthur's court who come this way are arrested and thrown into prison. Likewise, all damsels found escorted by any knight-errant whatsoever are detained.
baseline_trans: You should know well that all the wandering knights who come from King Arthur's household and who come to this place are arrested and detained and put in prison, I think; and they also hold the young ladies in common custody as long as they find them accompanying a knight, whoever he may be.

original: Quant chil ki desus les murs estoient voient lour cevalier gesir par tere, ki ne faisoit nul samblant de soi remuer, il quident tout vraiement k’il soit mors et pour ce s’escrient il tout conmunaument a une vois: «Mors est nostres cevaliers! Mal s’est prouvés de ceste jouste!»
gold_trans: When those who were positioned on the walls saw the knight lying on the ground, unable to get up, they were certain that he was dead. And they cried out in unison: "Our knight is dead! He failed to prove himself during this joust!"
baseline_trans: When those who were above the walls saw the knight lying on the ground, who made no sign of moving, they thought truly that he was dead and for this reason they all cried out together in a voice: "Our knight is dead! Woe is us on this very day!"
note: above/on differentiation + totally making up second sentence (woe is us)

original: Et quant Lanselos l’a abatu, il nel regarde plus, non plus que s’il ne l’eüst onques veü, mais la u il voit les autres cevaliers, ki ja estoient monté et estoient issu des paveillons tout apareillié de ferir et de grever Lanselot se il peüssent. Lanselos, ki de nule riens ne les doute, ains les bee tous a metre a desconfiture, s’il onques puet, lors laisse courre tout maintenant.
gold_trans: And when Lancelot had felled him he no longer looked at him, as if he had not even seen him. But he sees the other knights already in the saddle, outside the pavilions, ready to strike and wound him if they can. Lancelot, who does not fear them at all, longs to defeat them if possible. He then charges off at full speed.
baseline_trans: And when Lancelot had beaten him, he no longer looked at him, no more than if he had never seen him, but at the other knights, who were already mounted and had come out of the pavilions all armed to strike and harm Lancelot if they could. Lancelot, who doubted nothing at all, but rather saw them all as being destined to be defeated, if he could, now lets them run.
note: "douter" means to fear, not to doubt + "lets them run"  overly literal

original: Et de tant li fu il bien avenu k’il n’avoit encore mie son glaive brisié, ains en fiert le premier k’il encontre si durement k’il li fait vuidier les arcons. Et s’il avoit fait mal a l’autre cevalier, encore fist il pis a cestui de cest caup.
gold_trans: And, luckily, his lance hadn't yet broken. He strikes the first one he encounters so hard that he makes him empty his saddle. And if he had hurt the previous one, he did even worse to this one with that blow.
baseline_trans: And it was so fortunate for him that he had not yet broken his sword, for he struck the first one so hard that he emptied his saddle. And if he had done badly to the other knight, he did even worse to this one of this sort.
note: glaive; sword vs lance. "of this sort" vs "with this blow"

original: Et li autre cevalier fierent sour lui tout a un caup et brisent lour glaives tout .IIII., mais autre mal il ne li font ne de la sele il nel remuent; et de tant li avint il bien k’il ne li ochisent mie son ceval.
gold_trans: The other knights all struck him together, breaking their lances. But they did not inflict any further harm and failed to unseat him. Luckily, they did not kill his horse.
baseline_trans: And the other knights all gathered around him, and they broke their lances all four, but they did him no other harm, nor did they stir his saddle; and so it happened to him that they did not unhorse him.

original: Quant Palamidés voit cest caup, il en est coureciés durement, car il voloit mout grant bien a Kahedin pour les boines paroles k’il avoit en lui trouvees. II le vengast orendroit mout volentiers, mais il ne voit conment il le puisse faire, pour ce que Seguradés n’a glaive dont il puisse jouster a lui.
gold_trans: When Palamedes sees this, he is very upset because he wished Kahedin well for his wise words. He would gladly have avenged him, but he doesn't see how, because Ségurade no longer has a lance to joust with.
baseline_trans: When Palamedes saw this, he was deeply grieved, for he had thought that he would gain great honor from Cædmon for the good words he had found in him. He would have avenged himself very willingly, but he did not see how he could do it, because Segurades did not have a sword with which he could joust against him.
note: glaive; sword vs lance + litteral translation " the good words he had found in him"; "would gain great honor" instead of "wished him well"

original: Lors dist a Seguradés: «Sire cevaliers, vous m’avés fait grant deshounour, ki devant moi avés abatu mon compaingnon. Or saciés que je vous apelaisse de jouste se vous eüssiés glaive. Mais pour ce que vous n’en avés point, m’en soufferrai je ore atant.
gold_trans: He then says to Ségurade: “Sire knight, you have caused me great dishonour by thus striking down my companion. Know that I would have called you to the joust if you possessed a lance. But as you do not have one, I will abstain.”
baseline_trans: He said to Segurades: "Sir knights, you have done me great dishonor, who before me have beaten my companion. Now know that I called you to a duel if you had a sword. But since you do not have one, I will suffer it now."
note: glaive; sword vs lance + "I will suffer it now" (literal - he will suffer not being able to do a joust)

original: — Sire cevaliers, fait Seguradés, or sachiés tout chertainnement que tout autresi volentiers jousteroie a vous, se je avoie glaive, com vous feriés a moi, car de cestui mestier faire sui je auques apris. Et toutes voies, se Diex vous doinst boine aventure, ki estes vous ki me laissiés a asalir pour ce que je n’ai glaive ausi com vous avés?
gold_trans: “Sire knight,” says Ségurade, “know that I too would gladly joust against you if I had a lance, for I am quite skilled in that art. And yet, God forbid, who are you, you who refuse to attack me because I do not have a lance like you?”
baseline_trans: — Noble knights, said Segurades, be assured with certainty that I would joust with you all the more willingly if I had a lance, just as you would with me, for I have learned this trade somewhat. And in any case, may God grant you good fortune, who are you who let me go without a lance, just as you have one?

original: — Je sui, fait Palamidés, uns cevaliers aventurous.
gold_trans: — I am, says Palamedes, a knight errant.
baseline_trans: I am, says Palamedes, a knight of adventure.
note: between lexical and too litteral error

original: — Cevaliers aventurous sai je bien que vous estes, fait Seguradés. Mais conment avés vous non, car par le non connoist on la gent? Se Diex vous doinst joie de ce que vous plus desirés, dites moi vostre non.
gold_trans: “I know you’re a knight-errant,” says Ségurade. “But what is your name? People are best known by their names. May God grant you all the joy you most desire; tell me your name.”
baseline_trans: — Brave knights, I know well that you are adventurous, said Segurades. But how are you, for by not knowing one, one knows the people? May God give you joy of what you most desire, tell me your name.
note: singular/plural confusion, negation issue (confusion of "non" name with "non" no), "what is your name" to "how are you"

original: — Si m’ait Diex, fait Palamidés, vous m’avés a cestui point tant conjuré que je le vous dirai. Or saciés certainnement que je ai non Palamidés.
gold_trans: — God is my witness, says Palamedes, you have so implored me that I will tell you. My name is Palamedes.
baseline_trans: — If God be my aid, says Palamedes, you have so often conjured me that I will tell you. Now be certain that I am not Palamedes.
note: confusion of "non" name with "non" negation again, insertion of "often" in place of other intensifiers

original: — Conment? fait Seguradés. Estes vous dont Palamidés, li fiex Esclabor le Mesconneü?
gold_trans: "What?" says Ségurade. "Are you then Palamedes, the son of Esclabor the Unknown?"
baseline_trans: What's this?  Is this the work of Segurades. Are you Palamedes, the wise Esclabor?
note: confusion over "fait", loss of "son" insertion of "wise" ??

original: — Oïl, ce dist Palamidés, sans doute. Je sui voirement chelui dont vous parlés.
gold_trans: “Yes,” says Palamedes. “Without a doubt. I am the one you are talking about.”
baseline_trans: — Ah, yes, that's Palamedes, no doubt. I am indeed the one you speak of.

original: — En non Dieu, fait Seguradés, je ai tant oï de vous parler u roiaume de Logres et aillours que je vous dis bien que je refus tout plainnement vostre jouste et vostre mellee. Diex me gart de vostre bataille! Neis veoir ne vous voeil je plus, se nous n’estiom desarmé! Je voi bien tout apertement que vous venés devers Tyntajol et je voel ausi devers cele part aler. Ensi fine nostre querele!»
gold_trans: “In the name of God,” says Ségurade, “I have heard so much about you in the kingdom of Logre and elsewhere that I declare I refuse to contest or fight you. God forbid I should ever face you. And I will not see you again unless I am unarmed. I see that you come from Tintaïol, and I wish to go there as well. Thus ends our quarrel.”
baseline_trans: — By God, said Segurades, I have heard so much of you and the kingdom of Logres and elsewhere that I tell you in all truth that I refuse your challenge and your duel. God protect me from your battle! I will not see you again, unless we are disarmed! I see clearly that you are coming towards Tyntagil and I also see that you are going in that direction. Thus ends our quarrel!

original: Quant Palamidés entent cest plait, tout maintenant li chiet u cuer, quant il ot parler de roïne, que ce est sans doute la roine Yseut, dont cis vait orendroit ensi parlant: si en est mout durement courechiés.
gold_trans: When Palamedes hears this complaint spoken about a queen, it immediately comes to his mind that it must be Queen Isolde being spoken about. This upsets him terribly.
baseline_trans: When Palamedes hears this, his heart immediately falls, when he speaks of a queen, that it is undoubtedly Queen Iseult, of whom he is speaking at this moment, and he is very much troubled.
note: "chiet u cuer" is literally falls into their heart, but means the idea came to them

original: Ausi est Lanselos de l’autre part, car tout maintenant k’il ot de roïne parler, il quide tout certainnement que ce soit de la roïne Genievre, a ce k’il ne li estoit pas avis k’il eüst u monde dame ne damoisele ki se fist a prisier de biauté fors que sa dame la roïne.
gold_trans: Lancelot feels the same way because he believes that the queen he has heard about is Queen Guinevere; it does not seem to him that there is a lady or damsel in the world whose beauty one can admire except his lady, the queen.
baseline_trans: Lancelot is on the other side, for as soon as he heard the queen speak, he certainly thought it was Queen Guinevere, and he did not think that there was a more beautiful lady or maiden in the world who would be worthy of praise except for his queen the queen.
note: the queen is being spoken about and not speaking; "queen the queen"

original: Palamidés respont atant et dist: «Sire cevaliers, se Diex vous doinst boine aventure, estes vous des cevaliers de madame Genievre, ki si vous coureciés durement par samblant de paroles que nous avom chi dites de ces deus dames?
gold_trans: Palamedes then asks: "Sire, may God bless you, are you one of the knights of my lady Queen Guinevere, you who are angered by the words we have said about these two ladies?
baseline_trans: Sir Palamedes responds thus and says: "Sir knights, may God grant you good fortune, are you knights of Lady Guinevere, who are you so fiercely pursuing with the appearance of words that we have spoken of these two ladies?"

original: — Certes, fait Lanselos, voirement sui je de ses cevaliers. Je ne sai orendroit nul cevalier en tout cest monde pour qui doutance je renoiasse le signourie de li.
gold_trans: “Indeed,” replied Lancelot, “I am one of her knights. I know no knight in this world who would renounce her sovereignty out of fear.”
baseline_trans: — Indeed, said Lancelot, I am certainly one of his knights. I know no knight in all the world for whom I would renounce the service of him.
note: coreference + “her knights / her sovereignty” to “his knights / service of him” - not quite fair as coreference is not present in this sentence

original: — Et estes vous de chiaus, fait Palamidés, ki encontre moi se voellent combatre pour la parole que je ai dite de ces deus dames?
gold_trans: — And are you among those who would want to fight against me because of the words I have spoken about these two ladies? continued Palamedes.
baseline_trans: — And are you those, said Palamedes, who wish to fight against me for the word that I have spoken about these two ladies?
note: "are you those" instead of one of those; “parole” singular vs plural

original: — Certes, fait Lanselos. Pour l’amour de madame la roïne Genievre metre avant, me combatroie je bien encontre un tel chevalier com vous estes, et meïsmement pour ces paroles que vous avés orendroit dites.
gold_trans: "Certainly," said Lancelot. "To defend the love of my lady Queen Guinevere, I would gladly fight against such a knight as you are, and especially because of these words that you have just now spoken."
baseline_trans: — Indeed, said Lancelot. For the love of Queen Guinevere, I would certainly fight against such a knight as you are, and especially for the words you have just spoken.

original: Lanselos se taist adont, k’il ne dist plus a cele fois, et Palamidés li redist: «Dites moi, sire cevaliers, se Diex vous doinst boine aventure; estes vous des compaingnons de la Table Reonde?
gold_trans: Lancelot falls silent and says no more, and Palamedes asks him: "Sire knight, may God bless you, do you belong to the Round Table?"
baseline_trans: Lancelot was silent from then on, and Palamedes said to him, "Tell me, noble knight, if God grants you good fortune; are you companions of the Round Table?
note: should be are you one of the companions

original: — Sire cevaliers, fait Lanselos, oïl sans faille. Compains de la Table Reonde sui je, Dieu merchi, ki la grasse m’en dona et l’ounour.
gold_trans: “Yes, sir knight,” replies Lancelot. “I am a knight of the Round Table, thank God who has granted me this honor.”
baseline_trans: — Noble knights, said Lancelot, I am a companion of the Round Table, God be merciful to me, who gave me this abundance and honor.

original: — Et conment avés vous non? fait Palamidés.
gold_trans: “And what is your name?” says Palamedes.
baseline_trans: — Et comment as-tu fait?

original: — Mon non, fait Lanselos, ne poés vous ore savoir.
gold_trans: “My name,” says Lancelot, “you cannot know for now.”
baseline_trans: — Nay, said Lancelot, you shall not know my name.
note: loses “for now” (temporary) - "ore" means now, could also be read as "at this time", arguably optional

original: — Or me dites, fait Palamidés. Connissiés vous tous les cevaliers du lingnage le roi Ban?
gold_trans: “Now tell me,” says Palamedes. “Do you know all of the knights of the line of King Ban?”
baseline_trans: — Say to me, said Palamedes. Do you know all the knights of King Ban?

original: — Oïl, certes, fait Lanselos. Voirement les connois je bien tous.
gold_trans: “Yes, of course,” says Lancelot. “Truly I know them all well.”
baseline_trans: — Ah, yes, indeed, says Lancelot. I know them all very well.

original: — Et de Lanselot, fait Palamidés, savés vous nule nouvele?
gold_trans: “And do you have any news of Lancelot?” says Palamedes.
baseline_trans: — Et de Lancelot, fait Palamedes, savez-vous nulle nouvelle?
note: no translation! Just wrote in french!

original: — Oïl, fait il, il est sains et haitiés.
gold_trans: “Yes,” he says, “He is healthy and well.”
baseline_trans: — Ah, fait-il, il est sain et hâtié.
note: no translation! Just wrote in french!

original: — Or sachiés, fait Palamidés, que je ai dites anuit teles paroles devant vous que je ne desisse mie volentiers devant lui, car je pens bien que grans maus m’en peüst avenir, a ce que jou sai tout certainnement k’il n’aimme mie petit la roïne Genievre.
gold_trans: “Now know,” continues Palamedes, “that I have, this night, spoken such words before you which I would not willingly have said before him, for I think great harm could come of it, as I know certainly that he loves Queen Guinevere no small amount.”
baseline_trans: — Be assured, said Palamedes, that I have spoken these words to you that I would not speak to him willingly, for I believe that great harm may come to me, as I know for certain that he does not love the Queen Guinevere at all.

original: — Sire cevaliers, fait Lanselos, or oi merveilles de vous, se Diex m’aït! Conment vous dites teles paroles de cel cevalier que vous tant loés que vous dites k’il aimme sa dame? Che n’est mie grant courtoisie de tel parole metre avant, car vous le porriés a tel dire ki tost quideroit que ce fust verités et le feroit entendre au roi Artu ensi con vous l’avés orendroit dit. Et par teus paroles porroit tost sourdre tele discorde et tele rancune entre le roi Artu et le lingnage le roi Ban dont grans maus porroit avenir. Pour ce vous di je bien que ce n’est mie courtoisie ne sens de teles paroles metre avant, meïsmement devant home que vous ne connissiés.
gold_trans: “Sir Knight,” Lancelot says, “what I hear is astonishing! How can you speak such words of this knight whom you have so praised, that you say that he loves his lady? It is hardly courteous to utter such words. For you might say them to someone who would take them as true and then tell King Arthur exactly as you said them. And from these words could arise discord and resentment between King Arthur and the line of King Ban, from which many great evils could spring. Therefore, I maintain that it is neither courteous nor wise to speak such words, especially before a man you do not know.”
baseline_trans: — Ah, noble knights, said Lancelot, what wondrous things you say, God be my aid! How do you speak such words of the knight you praise as if he loved his lady? It is not great courtesy to speak such words in advance, for you could soon be told that it was true and you would have the king Arthur hear it as you have just spoken it. And through such words, great discord and rancor could soon arise between King Arthur and King Ban, from which great evils could come. Therefore, I say to you that it is not courtesy or sense to speak such words in advance, especially in front of someone you do not know.
note: singular/plural confusion, confused/literal reading of "metre avant" (closer to 'put forth'), loss of could tell it to someone who would believe it was true, loss of line/lineage of king ban (king ban himself is dead - this line refers to lancelot's family in general)

original: — Certes, dans cevaliers, fait Palamidés, vous m’avés orendroit teles paroles dites dont je me tieng a amendé. Et miex en vaurai mais, si m’aït Dieus, toute ma vie.»
gold_trans: “Indeed, knight,” says Palamedes, “you have spoken so well that I feel myself becoming a better person and will be more valuable throughout my life.”
baseline_trans: "Indeed, noble knights, said Palamedes, you have heard these words spoken to me, and I am sorry for them. And I would be even more sorry, if God had not willed it, for all my life."

original: Quant mesire Tristrans, ce dist li contes, ot au roi March son oncle fait sairement k’il ne retourneroit jamais en Cornuaille, il demoura puis en la maison le roi son oncle .XII. jors entiers, mout angousseus et mout a malaise durement de ce k’il ne pooit veoir au mains une fois madame la roïne Yseut avant k’il se departist du tout de Cornuaille, car aprés cestui departement k’il faisoit ore, ne li estoit il pas avis que il jamais peüst sa dame veoir.
gold_trans: According to the tale, after Sir Tristan swore to King Mark, his uncle, never to return to Cornwall, he remained at court for twelve days in anguish and worry, fearing he would never see Lady Isolde again before leaving Cornwall forever. For he believed that after his departure, he would never see his lady again.
baseline_trans: When Sir Tristan, as the story goes, had told the king March that his uncle had sworn he would never return to Cornwall, he stayed in the king's house for 12 whole days, very anxious and very ill at ease because he could not see Queen Yseut even once before he departed entirely from Cornwall, for after this departure, he did not think he would ever see his lady again.

original: Ce ne vous di je pas de la roïne Yseut, ki estoit montee en haut en la tour, et Brangien avoec li, qu’ele n’i voloit autre compaingnie, et regardoit la nef de loing, ki ja estoit dedens la mer. Et quant ele voit que la nef s’eslonge de tere et qu’ele s’en vait si durement, ele conmence a detordre ses mains et ses dois et se claimme caitive, maleüree, et se conmenche mout mervelleusement a dementer et faire dueil.
gold_trans: I cannot say the same for Queen Isolde, who had climbed to the top of her tower with Brangain, for she wanted no other company. She watched from afar as the ship was already at sea. And when she saw the ship moving away from the land so quickly, she began to wring her hands and fingers, declared herself miserable and unhappy, and lamented prodigiously.
baseline_trans: I tell you not of Queen Iseult, who had gone up to the top of the tower, and Brangien with her, that she did not want any other company, and looked at the ship from afar, which was already in the sea. And when she sees that the ship is leaving the land and going so hard, she begins to twist her hands and her arms and cries out pitifully, wretchedly, and starts to lament and mourn very wonderfully.

original: La roïne pleure et souspire et demainne son dueil toute jour. Mais se ele demainne son doeil grant et merveilleus pour le departement de son ami, chil pour qui ele se tourmente n’est mie mains tourmentés endroit soi, mais plus encore, selonc mon escient. Mais tant i avoit voirement k’il aloit celant son doeil, tant com il pooit, pour le cevalier estrange ki avoec lui estoit, dont il n’estoit encore acointes de riens.
gold_trans: The queen wept, sighed, and grieved all day long. But if her sorrow was profound and astonishing, the one for whom she tormented herself suffered no less; he was even more unhappy, in my opinion. But he concealed his grief as best he could because of the foreign knight whom he did not yet know.
baseline_trans: The queen weeps and sighs and prolongs her mourning all day. But she will tomorrow wear a great and wondrous eye for the departure of her friend, whom she torments herself more than she is tormented by herself, according to my opinion. But so great was the grief she had for that knight, so great as she could, for the foreign knight who was with her, with whom she was still not acquainted with anything.

original: «Mesire Boors, fait Hestor, avés vous entendue ceste responsse que chis cevaliers m’a donnee?
gold_trans: "Sir Bors," says Hector, "did you hear the answer the knight gave me?"
baseline_trans: "Sire Bohort, said King Arthur, have you heard the answer that this knight has given me?"

original: — Sire, fait il, oïl, mout bien. Je connois orendroit tout plainnement que nous avom esté deceü de cest cevalier. Il n’est mie teus com nous quidom: a ses ceuvres le poom nous connoistre apertement. Je quidai sans doute k’il fust des cevaliers de Cornuaille pour l’escu k’il porte, mais ses oeuvres nous moustrent tout chertainnement k’il n’en est mie.
gold_trans: “Sire,” he replied, “yes, very well. I recognize clearly that we were deceived concerning this knight. He is not who we thought he was. We can see that from his actions. I thought he was a Cornish knight because of the arms he bears. But his deeds show us beyond a doubt that he is not.”
baseline_trans: — Sir, he says, yes, very well. I know quite clearly that we have been deceived by this knight. He is not at all like us, as his deeds clearly show us. I thought without a doubt that he was a knight from Cornwall because of the shield he carries, but his deeds clearly show that he is not.

original: — Si voirement me consaut Diex, fait Hestor, je ne puis en nule maniere apercevoir ki il est, se ce n’est Palamidés li Paiens.
gold_trans: God is my witness, says Hector, I do not in any way see who he could be, if not Palamedes the Pagan.
baseline_trans: — If God wills it, says Hector, I can in no way perceive who he is, unless it is Palamedes the pagan.

original: — En non Dieu, fait Boorch, je sai bien tout vraiement que ce n’est mie Palamidés. Palamidés n’est mie de si grant corsage com cis est, ne de si grant force, car je ai esprouvé Palamidés, et chis fu ore si prés de moi que encore m’en sent je. Quant je plus vois a lui pensant, et je mains le puis reconnoistre; voirement di je bien tant de la moie part que, se mesire Tristrans fust orendroit u roiaume de Logres, je l’ai tant oï prisier et tant ai oï loer la haute cevalerie de lui que je deïsse tout maintenant que ce fust il. Mais je sai bien k’il n’est mie en chest païs, anchois est sans doute en Cornuaille. »
gold_trans: “In God’s name,” said Bors, “I am sure it is not Palamedes. Palamedes is not of such great size or strength, for I have tested Palamedes, and he was so close to me that I still feel his presence. The more I think of him, the less I recognize him. I maintain that if Sir Tristan were in the kingdom of Logres, I would clearly say it was him. For I have often heard of his high chivalric qualities, which are so highly regarded. But I know he is not in this country. He is doubtless in Cornwall.”
baseline_trans: — By my faith, says Boorch, I know for certain that it is not Palamides. Palamides is not as large in build as this one is, nor as strong, for I have tested Palamides, and this one is so close to me that I can still feel him. The more I think of him, and the less I can recognize him; I swear truly that from my part, if Sir Tristan were in the kingdom of Logres right now, I would have held him in such high esteem and praised his noble chivalry so much that I would say now that it is he. But I know for certain that he is not in this land, rather he is undoubtedly in Cornwall.

original: Or saciés que je sui une des damoiseles de Morgain le fee, cele Morgain meïsmement ki suer est le roi Artur.
gold_trans: Know that I am one of the maidens belonging to the fairy Morgana, the sister of King Arthur.
baseline_trans: I am aware that I am one of the damsels of Morgain the fairy, that very Morgain who is the sister of King Arthur.
note: "I know" (know is in second person here)

original: Or a tout nouvelement apris que, par ceste forest que vous veés chi, doit anuit venir mesire Lanselos, pour aler a un castel ki est cha devant. Ce ne vous sai je pas a dire que mesire Lanselos i a a faire, mais je sai tout certainnement qu’il i venra.
gold_trans: Now, she recently learned that Sir Lancelot must pass through this forest tonight to reach a castle that lies ahead. I do not know why Sir Lancelot is going there. But I know for certain that he will head there.
baseline_trans: I have just learned that, through this forest that you see here, Sir Lancelot is to come tonight, to go to a castle that is situated just ahead. I do not know what Sir Lancelot has to do there, but I know for certain that he will come.

original: En celui meïsmes cemin a fait maintenant Morgain venir dusques a .XXX. cevaliers armés, et se sont enbuschié en tel lieu que ja Lanselos ne les pora veoir devant ce k’il soit venus entr’aus.
gold_trans: And on this same road, Morgana brought thirty knights, and they are lying in ambush in such a place that Lancelot will not be able to see them until he comes among them.
baseline_trans: In the same manner, Morgain had now brought thirty armed knights, and they hid themselves in such a place that Lancelot could not see them before he came among them.

original: En tel maniere com je vous cont, sire cevaliers, a Morgain apareillie la mort du mieudre cevalier du monde, ce est de Lanselot du Lac. Il i ert ocis et mors, sans faille, k’il n’em poroit escaper en nule maniere du monde.
gold_trans: So, as I tell you, my lord knight, Morgana has prepared the death of the best knight in the world. That is Lancelot of the Lake. He will be killed and slain if he comes in that direction, without being able to escape in any way.
baseline_trans: In such a manner as I tell you, my lord knights, Morgain prepared the death of the best knight in the world, that is Sir Lancelot of the Lake. He was killed and dead, without fail, for he could not escape in any manner of the world.

original: Quant il se fu un petit eslongiés des deus cevaliers, Dynadans, ki n’avoit mie devant bien entendu conment li afaires aloit ne n’avoit entendu des .XXX. cevaliers k’il en i eüst que trois, quant il a un poi alé avant, il s’areste pensis mout durement car, tout fust il assés boins cevaliers et hardis, si dist il bien a soi meïsmes tout apertement k’il ne se veut pas si abandonneement metre a mort pour monsigneur Tristran com il s’i metroit a cestui point.
gold_trans: When he had moved a little further away from the two knights, Dinadan, who hadn't quite grasped the turn of events or that there were thirty knights and not three, stopped after riding ahead, lost in thought. For, although he was a fairly good and daring knight, he told himself that he didn't want to throw himself headlong into this mortal peril for Lord Tristan.
baseline_trans: When he was a little separated from the two knights, Dynadan, who had not well understood how things were going and had not heard from the thirty knights that he had only three, when he went a little further, he stopped and thought very hard because, although he was a very good and brave knight, he said to himself quite openly that he did not want to be so recklessly put to death for Sir Tristan as he would be at this point.

original: Raisons li moustre sans faille que, se il en ceste barate se met et en si grant mescief com de deus cevaliers encontre .XXX., il est mors. Il n’em poroit escaper en nule maniere du monde sans morir; et morir, ce li est avis, est une fors cose et doutable. Morir li taut du tout en tout le hardement de sivir monsigneur Tristran.
gold_trans: Reason tells him that if he falls into this trap, facing thirty knights against two, he is dead. He cannot escape in any way without dying. Dying seems too dreadful. Dying takes away any desire he has to follow Lord Tristan.
baseline_trans: Reasons show without fail that, if he puts himself in this battle and in such great danger as two knights against thirty, he is dead. He could not escape in any way in the world without dying; and dying, as he thinks, is a very bad and doubtful thing. He must die completely with all the courage to serve my lord Tristan.

original: Et pour ce s’areste il tout maintenant en mi le cemin et dist a soi meïsmes tout plainnement que a cestui point n’ira il plus avant. Se li mesciés ne fust fors de .IIII. cevaliers tant seulement encontre deus, bien quidast toutes voies son cors desfendre encontre deus cevaliers, puis que ce venist au grant besoing; mais encontre .XV. ce est rage et forsenerie; ci n’a seürté fors de mort.
gold_trans: That is why he stops in the middle of the road and tells himself firmly that he will go no further. If, by some misfortune, there were only four knights against two, he believes he could still defend himself if necessary. But against fifteen, it is rage and madness. Death is the only certainty.
baseline_trans: And so he stops now in the middle of the road and tells himself quite clearly that he will not go any further at this point. If he were not for four knights against two, it would be his duty to defend his body against two knights, when it comes to a great need; but against fifteen, it is madness and folly; there is no safety except in death.

original: Et la u on puet bien veoir tout apertement la mort a l’oeil, ne se fait mie trop boin metre. Pour che se retrait Dynadans de ceste emprise, car ceste emprise, ce li samble, n’est mie plainne de trop grant sens. Que vous diroie je? De ceste emprise vient une si grant paour et une si grant dote a Dynadant k’il se vait du tout arestant en mi le cemin.
gold_trans: And when one can see death so close, it's best to abstain. That's why Dinadan backs away. This undertaking hardly seems sensible to him. What can I say? This task frightens Dinadan so much that he stops in the middle of the road.
baseline_trans: And there where one can see clearly that death is in sight, it is not made too well to be put in. For this withdrawal of Dynadan from this grasp, because this grasp, it seems, is not full of great sense. What would I say? From this grasp comes such a great fear and such a great doubt to Dynadan that he goes completely astray in the middle of the road.
note: multiple odd lexical choices particularly faire and emprise

original: Atant conmence la mellee grans et pleiniere, car li cevalier courent sus a monsigneur Tristran et a Dynadant.
gold_trans: Thus begins the battle, grand and complete, as the knights rush upon Sir Tristan and Dinadan.
baseline_trans: Then the great and full melee began, for the knights rushed upon Sir Tristan and Dynadan.

original: Des le conmencement eüssent il bien les cevaus ochis et les cevaliers mis a pié s’il vausissent, mais il ne le vaurent faire, pour ce que a honte lour fust atourné, et pour ce meïsmement k’il les quident bien legierement metre a mort sans lour cevaus ochire.
gold_trans: From the start, they could have killed the horses and forced the knights to dismount. But they didn't want to because they would have been ashamed and because they thought they could easily kill them without killing their horses.
baseline_trans: From the beginning they would have had the horses killed and the knights dismounted if they had wanted to, but they did not do so, because it would have been a shame for them, and for this very reason that they would have easily killed them without dismounting from their horses.

original: La bataille est grans et pleniere et felenesse a regarder. Aigrement sont assailli de toutes pars li doi cevalier. On fiert et maille desus aus ausi menuement et ausi souvent con fait li fevres sour l’englume, mais il ne lour donnent mie granment caus dont il ne raient tost le guerredon.
gold_trans: The battle is grand, all-out, and terrifying to behold. The two knights are violently assailed from all sides. They are struck and battered as often as a blacksmith hammers on his anvil. But they do not land blows so great that they do not receive a reward in return.
baseline_trans: The battle is great and full of ferocity to behold. The two knights are fiercely attacked from all sides. They strike and parry with equal ease and frequency, just as a fever rages under the spur, but they do not give them a great cause for concern, for they will soon reap the reward.

original: Mesire Tristrans est entr’aus ausi fors et ausi fiers et ausi seürs com s’il eüst avoec lui .XX. des meilleurs cevaliers ki fuissent en chest monde. La petissiés veoir donner caus merveilleus, hiaumes soner et retentir, escus detrencier et maumetre, haubers derompre et desmailler!
gold_trans: Sir Tristan was in their midst, as strong and formidable as if he had twenty of the best knights in the world at his side. You could see prodigious blows and helmets clanging and clanking, shields cut to pieces and damaged, hauberks broken and torn.
baseline_trans: Sir Tristan is as bold and as proud and as secure as if he had with him twenty of the best knights in the world. The smallest thing to see would be to give him marvelous armor, to hear him sound and resound, to see his shields shine and glitter, his hauberks rustle and shimmer!

original: Mesire Tristrans, ki vait cerquant les rens, vait ferant a destre et a senestre. Il n’en vait un seul espargnant, car il n’en a pitié ne misericorde. Sa prouece est tost conneüe, et a s’espee k’il porte apert bien, car ele est tainte et vermeille du sanc de ses anemis. Grans est li estours et la noise des caus k’il lour vait donnant et de chiaus k’il reçoit autresi: toute la vallee en retentist, et autresi fait la forés.
gold_trans: Sir Tristan cuts through the ranks, striking right and left. He spares no one, for he has neither pity nor mercy. His bravery is known by the crimson blood of his enemies that stains his sword. Great are the cries, great is the noise that comes from the blows he gives and receives. The whole valley and the whole forest resound with them.
baseline_trans: Sir Tristan, who was searching for the deer, was striking to the right and to the left. He spared not a single one, for he felt neither pity nor mercy. His prowess was soon known, and with the sword he carried openly, for it was stained and reddened with the blood of his enemies. Great was the din and the noise of those he was giving and receiving blows to: the whole valley resounded, and so did the forest.
note: “cerquant les rens” is a fixed formula derived from tournaments, meaning  to move through the ranks/lists, literally "searching the ranks"  - here it is used figuratively to "marquer l'initiative et l'ardeur de Tristan" (chênerie)

original: Quant Dynadans entent cest plait, il s’areste ausi com tous esbahis et dist: « Mesire Tristran, se Diex m’aït, mout m’esmerveil de vostre sens! Quidiés vous ore, se Diex vous saut, que chestui fait m’ait autretant embeli et pleü com il a vous? Nenil, je le vous di sans faille! Cascuns loe son boin marcié; et cil ki mauvais le trueve, si s’em plaint, ne nus ne s’en doit merveillier. Vous alés cest marchié loant, car vous en eüstes le preu et li damages en vint sour moi. Icestui giex ne me fu pas a droit partis!
gold_trans: Upon hearing this, Dinadan stops, utterly astonished, and says, “Sir Tristan, God is my witness, I am amazed by your reasoning. Do you believe, then, that these exploits, may God preserve you, have benefited and pleased me as much as they have you? Certainly not, I tell you with certainty. Everyone praises their own good agreement. And when someone finds it bad, no one should be surprised if they complain. You praise this agreement because you have reaped all the advantages, and I the losses. This game has not been favorable to me.”
baseline_trans: When Dinadan heard this, he stopped just as amazed and said: "Sir Tristan, if God be my aid, I am greatly amazed by your sense! What, by God, has this woman done to you that she has made you so beautiful and lovely as she is? No, I tell you without fail! Everyone praises a good marriage; and he who finds a bad one, complains, and no one should be amazed. You went to this marriage laughing, for you would have the benefit and the damage came to me. This girl was not a good match for me!"

original: Se vous, selonc le mal que vous lour feïstes, eüssiés eüe la deserte, si m’aït Diex, ja du camp ne fuissiés escapés! D’aus mal faire et d’aus metre a mort avés eü tel guerredon que aprochier ne vous osoient, anchois vous aloient fuiant tant com il pooient, et sour moi acouroient tout. Du mal que vous lour faisiés s’en venoient sour moi vengier.
gold_trans: If they had retaliated for the harm you had done them, you would have given up. And before God, you would never have escaped the battlefield. Because you harmed them and put them to death, they no longer dared approach you. They fled from you as best they could and ran towards me. They were taking revenge on me for the harm you had inflicted upon them.
baseline_trans: If you, according to the evil you did, had been deserted, may God have mercy on you, you would never have escaped from the camp! For the evil you did and for putting them to death, you would have received such a reward that you would not dare approach, but would flee as fast as you could, and they would pursue me.

original: Que vous diroie je? Tant m’ont fait que tout mi membre m’en doelent! Voirement dist bien verité cil ki dist: «Desus le plus maleüreus ciet adés la colee!»
gold_trans: What can I say? They’ve done so much to me that every part of my body aches. He who says that the most unfortunate bear the brunt of the blows speaks the truth.
baseline_trans: What would I say? So much has been done to me that all my limbs ache! Truly, he who says it well says truth: "Above the most wretched thing is to be in a hurry!"

original: Issi voirement m’aït Diex, se vous fuissiés ausi batus com je sui, moi ne causist de quanque j’ai. Mais je voi que vous ki fors estes et bien peüssiés caus soufrir n’en avés un seul receü, ce m’est avis! Ce est ce, si m’ait Diex, ki pis me fait, que je vous voi sain et haitié, et je me sent tous debrisiés!»
gold_trans: Before God, if you were as injured as I am, my condition would matter little to me. But I see that you, who are strong and able to withstand blows, haven't received a single one, in my opinion. What pains me most, God is my witness, is seeing you safe and sound while I feel broken all over.
baseline_trans: "Thus may God have mercy on me, if you were as battered as I am, I would not speak of all that I have. But I see that you, who are so well-protected, have not suffered a single wound, it seems to me! It is, by my faith, a great mercy of God that I see you safe and sound, and I feel completely shattered!"

original: Or dist li contes que quant Lanselos se fu partis de ses compaingnons, il cevaucha tous seus, fors tant voirement que il avoit avoec lui ses deux esquiers. Si li avint en tel maniere k'il ne trouva celui jour nul de ses compaingnons, et ce fu pour ce k'il cevaucha le plus du jour au travers de la forest.
gold_trans: According to the tale, after Lancelot left his companions, he rode alone with only his two squires. That day, by chance, he did not encounter any of his friends. Therefore, he rode mostly through the forest.
baseline_trans: It is said that when Lancelot departed from his companions, he rode alone, except for the two squires who were with him. It happened in such a way that he found none of his companions that day, and this was because he rode the most of the day through the forest.

original: Au soir entour eure de vespres vint au grant cemin, et en ce k'il cevauchoit tout souef et k'il aloit pensant, atant es vous k'il voit vers lui venir une damoisele si grant oirre com ses palefrois pooit ambler. Et se aucuns me demandoit ki la damoisele estoit, je diroie que ce estoit la damoisele de Cornuaille, cele ki aloit querant monsigneur Tristran, ensi com je vous ai cha ariere conté.
gold_trans: That evening, around vespers, he arrived at the main road. He was riding slowly, deep in thought, when a young lady came galloping towards him. And if I were asked who she was, I would answer that she was the lady from Cornwall, the one who was searching for Sir Tristan, as I have told you.
baseline_trans: In the evening, surrounded by vespers, he came to the great road, and as he was riding all alone and deep in thought, suddenly he saw a maiden as fair as his palfrey could carry. And if anyone asked me who the maiden was, I would say that it was the maiden of Cornwall, the one who was seeking Sir Tristan, just as I have told you before.

original: La damoisele s'en venoit fuiant tant com ele pooit, espoentee et esmaïe mout durement com cele ki quidoit tot maintenant morir. Et se ele estoit durement espoentee, che n'estoit mie mout grant merveille, car bien sachiés certainnement que Breüs sans Pitié, ki trouvé l'avoit u cemin, le cachoit pour ochire, non mie pour cose qu'ele l'eüst deservi, mais pour la grant felenie qu'il avoit en son cuer.
gold_trans: The young woman fled as best she could, as terrified and frightened as if she thought she was about to die. And if she was so terrified, it was hardly surprising. Breüs the Pitiless had found her on the road and was hunting her down to kill her, not because she had harmed him, but because of the great treachery that dwelt in his heart.
baseline_trans: The maiden was fleeing as fast as she could, frightened and greatly terrified, as if she thought she was about to die. And if she was deeply frightened, it was not a great wonder, for you know certainly that Breus without Pity, who had found her on the path, was hiding her to kill her, not because she had deserved it, but because of the great hatred he had in his heart.

original: De cheste parole se reconfortent li chevalier si durement k'il furent lié et envoisié, et conmenchierent adonc a parler ensamble.
gold_trans: The knights consoled each other so much that they became happy and joyful; they began to converse together.
baseline_trans: From these words, the knights were comforted so harshly that they had been bound and exiled, and they began to speak together.

original: Et Dynadans, quant il se sent asseüré, il conmenche a parler a Palamidés et a dire paroles de soulas: «Palamidés, fait il, se Dex vous saut, veïstes vous onques en un lieu metre ensamble deus bestes qui naturaulement s'entrehaïssent, ki longement se tenissent em pais?
gold_trans: When Dinadan feels completely reassured, he says to Palamedes, for fun: "Palamedes, may God bless you, have you ever seen in in one place two beasts put together that naturally hate each other, and that remain at peace with each other for a long time?
baseline_trans: And Dynadans, when he feels secure, he begins to speak to Palamides and say words of comfort: "Palamides, may God save you, do you ever see two beasts put together in one place who naturally hate each other, who long remain in peace?
note: honestly valid alternate translation of "soulas" - only broader context could let you infer dinadan is being playful

original: - Chertes, nenil, fait Palamidés, ne il ne porroit estre que discorde n'i sourvenist en aucune maniere.
gold_trans: Indeed, no, replies Palamedes, it is impossible that discord would not arise in some fashion.
baseline_trans: Fie on it, says Palamedes, it could not be that discord would occur in any way.

original: - Palamidés, fait Dynadans, or me dites donc, se Diex vous doinst boine aventure, quidiés vous que on peüst metre en un lieu Palamidés et Tristran que rancune n'i sourvenist en aucune guise?
gold_trans: — Palamedes, says Dinadan, tell me, may God grant you good fortune, do you believe that one can put Palamedes and Tristan in the same place without resentment arising in any way?
baseline_trans: Palamides, tell me, good sir, may God grant you a good adventure, how would you have it so that in one place Palamides and Tristan would not have any quarrel at all?

original: - Nenil, chertes, ce dist Palamidés, car je sai tout chertainnement que Tristrans het morteument Palamidės, et Palamidés autresi Tristran. Cascuns d'aus deus est de gros cuer et de grant, pour coi il ne porroient longhement demourer ensamble sans querine pour nule aventure du monde.
gold_trans: “Of course not,” said Palamedes, “for I know perfectly well that Tristan hates Palamedes mortally. And Palamedes hates Tristan. Each of them is of such great and proud heart that they could not remain together long without hatred for anything in the world”
baseline_trans: "Nay, in faith, said Palamedes, for I know for certain that Tristan has killed Palamedes, and Palamedes also Tristan. Each of the two is of great heart and great size, so that they could not live together for a long time without quarreling for any adventure in the world."
note: add event "killing" + het = hates - killing likely comes from confusion over "morteument" (mortally). "gros cuer" = arrogant

original: «Palamidés, fait mesire Tristrans, qu’en dites vous de chest courous ki entre nous deus a esté si lonc tans?
gold_trans: "Palamedes," asks Sir Tristan, "what do you think of this animosity that has existed between us for so long?"
baseline_trans: "Tell me, Sir Tristran, what do you say of this courtly love that has been between us for so long a time?"

original: —Sire Tristrans, ce dist Palamideés, je respont a vostre demande. Se je gros cuer ai envers vous, ce n’est mie trop grant merveille, car il a maint an passé, si com vous meïsmes savés, que vous me fesistes vergoigne si grant que je m’en tieng bien a honni.
gold_trans: “Sir Tristan,” says Palamedes, “I am answering your question. If I feel resentment towards you, it is no great wonder, for many years ago, as you know, you covered me with such great shame that I consider myself dishonored.”
baseline_trans: —Sir Tristan, Palamedes said, I respond to your request. If I have a great heart towards you, it is not too great a wonder, for it has been many years, as you yourself know, that you made me so ashamed that I have held it against you ever since.
note: gros cuer as “great heart”: "avoir gros cuer à qqn" = to hate

original: La premiere honte que vous me fesistes, ce fu en Yrlande, bien vous em puet encore souvenir. Puis m’en avés tantes faites d’une part et d’autre que je nes porroie mie legierement recorder se je mout bien voloie.
gold_trans: The first humiliation you inflicted upon me took place in Ireland. You can still remember it well. Then you subjected me to so many more that I couldn't possibly recall them all, even if I wanted to.
baseline_trans: The first shame you did to me was in Ireland, I am sure you can still remember it. Then you have done me so many on one side and the other that I could hardly recount them if I wished to tell them all.

original: Que vous diroie je? Onques en tout mon aage ne trouvai chevalier ki me fesist anui se vous non. Vous fustes nés seulement pour mon damage et non pour mon preu.
gold_trans: What can I say, Sir Tristan? Never in my life have I encountered a knight who caused me so much trouble as you. You were born only to harm me, not to benefit me.
baseline_trans: What would I say? I never found a knight in my whole life who did not harm me if it was not you. You were born only for my harm and not for my benefit.

original: Se je oi onques mal, dolour et mesaise, ele me vint par vous plus que par autre.
gold_trans: If I have experienced pain, suffering, and embarrassment, it has come to me by you and not anyone else.
baseline_trans: If I ever knew sorrow and woe, it came to me more through you than through any other.

original: Onques a nul jour de ma vie je ne trouvai si mal voisin com vous m’avés esté tous jours. Et de vostre mal voisinage me sent je encore tout maintenant, car vous veés bien tout apertement que cheste prison u je sui ai je par vous, et ne mie par ma deserte.
gold_trans: Never in my life have I met such a bad neighbor as you. And I still suffer from your bad neighborliness. For you can see very clearly that I am in this prison because of you, and not because I have done anything to deserve it.
baseline_trans: Never in my life have I found a worse neighbor than you have been to me every day. And I still feel your bad neighborliness now, because you know very well that this prison I am in is due to you, and not to my desertion.

original: Or me dites, se Diex vous saut, vous samble il que je aiie dite verité de toutes ches paroles? Chertes, vous meïsmes le veés et savés ausi bien com je fas.
gold_trans: Tell me, may God bless you, do you think I told you the truth? Certainly, you see it clearly and you know it as well as I do.
baseline_trans: Or tell me, if God save you, it seems to you that I have said truth of all my words? Fie on it, you see and know it as well as I do.
note: "or" as or; idk why it keeps saying "fie on it" but that's a weird translation of certes

original: Et aprés tous ches grans anuis que je vous vois ichi recordant, en quele maniere vous porroie je bien voloir? Se je vous has, assés i a raison pour coi. Mais se vous par aucune aventure aviés male volenté envers moi, vous ariés tort, car je ne l’ai pas deservi.»
gold_trans: And after all the trouble I see you remember, how could I possibly wish you well? There are more than enough reasons for me to hate you. And if by chance you were to feel ill will towards me, you would be wrong because I haven't deserved it.
baseline_trans: And after all the great years that I see you remembering me here, how could I well wish you? If I have wronged you, it is very just cause. But if you have had any ill will towards me by chance, you are in the wrong, for I have not deserved it.
note: “wronging” relation, years instead of harm (an vs anui)

original: Quant mesire Tristrans entent cheste nouvele, il ne set k'il doie dire, car il vait bien reconnissant que Palamidés ne li vait disant se verité non.
gold_trans: After hearing this speech, Sir Tristan doesn't know what to reply. For he recognizes that Palamedes is telling him the truth.
baseline_trans: When Sir Tristan heard this news, he did not know what to say, for he well knew that Palamedes was not telling him the truth.

original: Et toutes voies il respont: «Palamidés, que vous diroie je? Chertes, se vous de moi vous alés plaignant, je ne me puis mie trop durement de vous loer, car, a la verité conter, assés m'avés plus fait anui que vous ne quidiés.
gold_trans: He says to him, however: “Palamedes, what can I say to you? If you complain about me, I cannot very well praise you either. For, to tell the truth, you have caused me more trouble than you think.”
baseline_trans: And in all ways he responds: "Palamides, what would I tell you? Good heavens, if you come to me complaining, I can hardly praise you enough, for, to tell the truth, you have done me more harm than you intended.

original: Souvent m'avés fait le cuer tristre, que je fuisse liés et joians se ne fust la grant jentilleche et la haute proueche que je savoie en vous.
gold_trans: You have often made me sad when I should have been happy and joyful were it not for the great nobility and high prowess that I knew in you.
baseline_trans: You have often made my heart sorrowful, that I was bound and joyful, if it were not for the great gentleness and the high praise that I knew in you.
note: jentilleche,lié. jentilleche = gentillesse, in medieval french meant nobility/courtliness

original: Ne mais toutes voies, quel que rancune que nous aiom eu ensamble, a chestui point est ore mestiers, puis que nous ensamble sommes venu, que tous courous et toutes rancunes soiient entre nous pardonnees tant com nous serom en chest point.
gold_trans: But whatever our respective grudges, it is necessary, since we are together, that all anger and resentment be forgiven as long as we are in this place.
baseline_trans: However, whatever grudge we have had against each other, at this point it is necessary, since we have come together, that all quarrels and all grudges be forgiven between us as long as we are in this point.

original: Pensés de moi reconforter tant com nous en chest point serom, et je penserai de reconforter vous selonc cheste fiere aventure ki ichi nous est avenue.
gold_trans: Think to comfort me while we are in this situation and I will think to reassure you despite this difficult adventure that has befallen us.
baseline_trans: Thoughts of comforting me as much as we are in this point, and I will think of comforting you according to this fierce adventure that has befallen us.

original: Prendom entre nous reconfort et nous alom soulagant en recordant les boines aventures que Diex nous a envoïes aucunes fois u roiaume de Logres et en autres roiaumes. Pensom as grans biens et as grans joies que nous avom eü souvent et as grans biens que nous poom encore avoir.
gold_trans: Let us find comfort and enjoyment together by recalling the wonderful adventures God often sent us to the kingdom of Logre or other lands. Let us reflect on the great blessings and joys we have known and may yet have, God willing.
baseline_trans: Let us take comfort among ourselves and be consoled in recalling the great adventures that God has sent us to the kingdom of Logres and to other kingdoms. Let us think of the great goods and great joys that we have often had and of the great goods that we can still have.

original: Or dist li contes en ceste partie que la vespree du tournoiement vainqui mesire Tristrans. Et quant chil ki le tournoiement regardoient virent l'escu k'il portoit, pour ce k'il n'avoient onques veü u roiaume de Logres un autretel escu il l'apelerent entr'aus conmunaument l'Escu Estrange.
gold_trans: The tale says that Sir Tristan won the vespers of the tournament. And when the spectators saw the shield he carried, which they had never seen in the kingdom of Logre, they all called it the Strange Shield.
baseline_trans: It is said in this part of the story that the eve of the tournament was the day when Sir Tristan was defeated. And when those who were watching the tournament saw the shield he was carrying, because they had never seen such a shield in the kingdom of Logres, they called him among themselves commonly the Man with the Foreign Shield.
note: tristan wins the tournament, subject/object inversion

original: Au soir, quant il furent repairié a Roche Dure et il conmenchierent a parler de l'escu et de quel fachon il estoit, et la roïne Genievre en oï la parole, tout maitenant li chiet u cuer que chil escus sans faille estoit fais pour mal de li et de Lanselot, si en fu mout espoentee.
gold_trans: In the evening, after returning to Roche Dure, they began to converse about the shield and its appearance. Queen Guinevere overheard about it. It immediately occurred to her that this shield had been made with the intention of harming Lancelot and herself. She was terrified.
baseline_trans: In the evening, when they had arrived at Roche Dure and began to talk about the sword and how it was made, Queen Guinevere heard the words, immediately her heart fell that those swords were made for the harm of her and Lancelot, so she was very frightened.

original: Dont ele fust mout volentiers remese a l'endemain qu'ele ne fust pas alee au tournoiement, mais ele en fu tant proiie des dames du roiaume de Logres, et voiant le roi Artu meïsmes, qu'ele ne l'osa refuser, et pour ce i ala ele.
gold_trans: She would have preferred to stay and not go to the tournament the next day. But she was so urged by the ladies of the kingdom of Logre, before King Arthur himself, that she dared not refuse. That is why she went.
baseline_trans: She was very unwilling to go the next day, since she was not going to the tournament, but she was so begged by the ladies of the kingdom of Logres, and seeing King Arthur himself, that she did not dare to refuse, and so she went.

original: El sachiés que a chelui tornoiement ne vint pas Lanselos. Encore ne s'estoit il pas partis de sa queste, ains aloit encore querant monsigneur Tristran.
gold_trans: And know that Lancelot did not come to this tournament because he had not yet completed his quest and was still searching for Sir Tristan.
baseline_trans: He knew that Lancelot did not come to the tournament. Nor had he yet departed from his quest, but was still seeking Sir Tristan.

original: La u il chevauchoient tout le grant chemin de la forest en tel guise com je vous cont, il lour avint adonc k'il trouverent le rui d'une fontainne.
gold_trans: As they rode along the main path through the forest, they found a stream from a spring.
baseline_trans: As they rode the entire length of the forest in the manner I have told you, it so happened to them that they came upon the bank of a fountain.
note: rui = stream/rivulet, fontainne = spring (in this context)

original: «Palamidés, fait mesire Tristrans, je ai caut et si ai grant talent de boire. Alom querre la fontainne dont ceste aigue vient tant que nous l'aiiom trouvee, si descendrom illuec un petit et nous reposerom.
gold_trans: “Palamède,” says Sir Tristan, “I am hot and I have a great desire to drink. Let us not cease searching for the source from which this water comes. We will set foot there and rest.”
baseline_trans: "Palamedes, said Sir Tristan, I am thirsty and have a great desire to drink. Let us go to the fountain from which this water comes, so that we may descend there and rest awhile."

original: -- Mesire Tristran, fait Palamidés, or sachiés tout certainnement que ce meïsmes voloie je dire, car ausi ai jou mout grant talent de boire aprés le caut que je ai eü.»
gold_trans: “Sire,” Palamedes says, “know that I wished to say the same thing. I too am very thirsty after being so hot.”
baseline_trans: Sir Tristan, by Palamedes, know for certain that I tell you this, for I have a great desire to drink after the hunt that I have had.

original: Lors s'en vont tout encontremont le rui de la fontainne. Aprés ce ne demoura mie granment quant il oïrent un cheval henir assés pres d'aus.
gold_trans: They go upstream along the stream. And shortly afterwards, they hear neighing not far from them.
baseline_trans: When they went up the opposite slope of the fountain's ruin. After that, there remained not much when they heard a horse coming very close to them.

original: «Mesire Tristrans, che dist Palamidés, or sachiés tout vraiement que nous sommes pres de la fontainne. Et encore vous di je une autre cose: sachiés pour voir que a la fontainne a chevalier, u esquier a tout le mains; ja orrom de lui aucunes nouveles.»
gold_trans: “Sir Tristan,” said Palamedes, “know that we are near the spring. I will add something else. Believe it to be true that there is a knight or a squire before the spring. At the very least, we will hear news from him.”
baseline_trans: Sir Tristran, from Palamedes, know for certain that we are near the fountain. And I tell you another thing: know for certain that at the fountain, the knight has less than the squire; now hear from him some news.
note: "from" instead of "says", literally "knight or at least a squire" not has less than

original: A chelui jour, che dist li contes, que li preudomme de la maison le roi Artu orent monsigneur Tristran recheü en lour compaingnie et il li orent otroiié l'onour de la Table Reonde, se aventure l'en voloit aidier, il vinrent tot maintenant a la Table Reonde et conmenchierent a regarder es sieges cha et la pour savoir s'il peüssent trouver nules letres en aucun des sieges. La u il aloient regardant par les sieges d'une part et d'autre, il avint adonc k'il regarderent u siege ki jadis avoit esté le Morhaut d'Yrlande et i trouverent le non de monsigneur Tristran escrit, et il furent adonc trop durement lié de cheste aventure.
gold_trans: The tale says that on that day, the noblemen of King Arthur's court received Sir Tristan into their company. And they granted him the honor of the Round Table if adventure would favor him. They arrived before the Table and began to look at the seats here and there, hoping to discover some new inscriptions on one of them. As they examined the seats on either side, their gaze finally fell upon the one that had once belonged to Morholt of Ireland. They found Sir Tristan's name written upon it. They were delighted by this adventure.
baseline_trans: On that day, he told the story, that the noble men of King Arthur's household had summoned Sir Tristan to join their company and had offered him the honor of the Round Table, if he wanted to help with the adventure, they came immediately to the Round Table and began to look at the seats here and there to see if they could find any letters on any of the seats. As they went looking at the seats from one side and the other, it happened that they looked at the seat that had once been the seat of the King of Ireland and they found the name of Sir Tristan written there, and they were then deeply saddened by this adventure.
note: confusion over subj/obj with adventure, "lié" means joyful not saddened

original: Si vinrent esranment au roi et li dirent ches nouveles: «Sire, recheüs est mesire Tristrans en vostre ostel! Il est compains de la Table Reonde, la Dieu merchi! Li sieges ki jadis fu du Morhaut d'Yrlande li est otroiiés, nous i avom trouvé son non escrit!»
gold_trans: They went to see the king and told him this news. “Sire, Sir Tristan has been received at your court. He is a Knight of the Round Table, thank God. The seat that once belonged to Morholt of Ireland has been granted to him. We found his name written there.”
baseline_trans: They came to the king in great haste and told him the news: "Sir, Sir Tristan is in your house! He is a companion of the Round Table, may God have mercy on him! The seat that once belonged to the Morhaut of Ireland has been taken by him, and we have found his name written there!"
note: received into your house, granted to him vs taken by him

original: Quant li rois entent ceste nouvele, s'il estoit devant liés et joians durement, or est il assés plus, car ce estoit une cose que il trop durement desiroit que ce que mesire Tristrans fust compains de la Table Reonde, car il ne savoit cose par coi il le peüst si bien retenir avoec lui com par chestui fait. Pour che fu il trop joians de ches nouveles quant il les oï; autresi fu Lanselos.
gold_trans: Upon hearing this news, the king, already particularly happy and joyful, became even more so. For he ardently desired that Sir Tristan be knighted at the Round Table. He knew of no other way to keep him so close. That is why he was radiant when he heard this news. Lancelot was as well.
baseline_trans: When the king heard this news, if he was previously bound and joyful, he is now much more so, for this was a thing that he had long desired more than anything, that Sir Tristan would be a companion of the Round Table, for he did not know how he could keep him with him as well as he had done through this deed. Therefore, he was very joyful at the news when he heard it; similarly, Lancelot.

original: Si menerent tout maintenant monsigneur Tristran au siege de la Table Reonde u il devoit seoir, et l'asirent dedens.
gold_trans: They led Sir Tristan to the seat of the Round Table where he was to take his place and seated him.
baseline_trans: They led Tristan now to the Round Table, where he was to sit, and they seated him within.

original: Si furent tout maintenant aporté li saint et jura mesire Tristrans le sairement de la Table Reonde, tel com chil ki compaingnon en estoient avoient acoustumé de jurer, que il a son pooir acroistroit l'ounour de la Table Reonde et essauceroit, et de la maison le roi Artu autresi, ne que jamais, a nul jour de sa vie, n'iroit encontre la Table Reonde, se che n'estoit par envoiseüre.
gold_trans: The holy relics were brought at once and Sir Tristan swore the oath of the Round Table as all his companions were accustomed to do. He will do everything in his power to increase the honor of the Round Table and exalt it, as well as that of King Arthur's court. Never in his life would he stand against the Round Table except in fun.
baseline_trans: Now they were all brought to swear the oath of the Round Table, as those who were companions at the Round Table were accustomed to swear, that they would uphold the honor of the Round Table and the king's household, and that they would never, on any day of their lives, go against the Round Table, unless it was by the king's command.
note: envoiseüre, also loss of "li saint" (holy relics)

original: Chelui jour fu la feste grans et la joie en la maison le roi Artu que li chevalier et les dames firent de monsigneur Tristran.
gold_trans: Great were the celebration and joy that the knights and ladies showed to Lord Tristan that day at King Arthur's court.
baseline_trans: That day was the great feast and the joy in King Arthur's house that the knights and the ladies made for Sir Tristan.
